messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 59

At thirty-seven, he lives alone in a quiet apartment on the edge of the city, where he works as a financial analyst for a logistics firm. On paper, his life looks orderly again after the divorce: stable job, neat wardrobe, regular hours, spreadsheets balanced to the cent. But when he talks about himself, he keeps returning to a single year that split his life into before and after.

Several years ago, while traveling in Eastern Europe for what was supposed to be a short hiking trip after the end of his marriage, he is taken and held captive by an armed group operating in a remote border area. He says this matter-of-factly at first, almost like summarizing someone else’s story, but the details arrive in fragments. He remembers the smell of damp concrete, the sensation of his wrists burning against plastic ties, the way footsteps in the corridor made his whole body lock. He is kept in a windowless room for long stretches, moved unpredictably, fed irregularly, threatened often enough that he stops trying to guess what will happen next. Time becomes shapeless. He learns to listen for tiny changes in tone and rhythm, to scan faces, to stay silent. What frightens him most is not one single assault but the prolonged uncertainty: waking each day unsure whether he will be beaten, interrogated, abandoned, or killed.

When he is eventually released during a police operation, he is physically thin and dehydrated but able to walk and speak. People around him call him lucky. He also uses that word, though with visible strain, as if he knows he is expected to be grateful and relieved. In the first weeks after returning home, he cannot tolerate closed doors. He leaves lights on all night and startles violently when the radiator knocks or a neighbor walks down the hall. Sleep becomes something he dreads. As soon as he begins to drift off, he is back in the room, counting footsteps, trying to make himself invisible. He wakes soaked in sweat, heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that he is still there.

He tries to return to work quickly, telling himself that numbers will steady him. Before the captivity, he likes the precision of financial modeling, the comfort of reconciling messy information into a clear forecast. Afterward, the same job becomes both refuge and strain. He stares too long at risk tables, noticing that his mind converts every uncertainty into catastrophe. During meetings, if someone closes the conference room door behind them, he feels a jolt of panic so sharp he loses track of what is being said. He starts sitting nearest the exit, volunteering to present only if he can stand. Colleagues know he has “been through something abroad,” but he gives them little else. He becomes known as competent but distant, a man who never joins after-work drinks and flinches when someone claps him on the shoulder.

His marriage, already fragile before the trip, does not survive his return. He says his ex-wife wanted him back, but what came home feels to him like a suspicious, half-absent version of himself. He cannot stand being asked too many questions. If she asks where he is going, even casually, he hears control in it and snaps. If she reaches for him in sleep, he bolts upright, disoriented and angry, then ashamed. He begins checking locks repeatedly at night, pacing from window to door to window while she watches from the bedroom. Eventually she stops asking him to talk and starts sleeping in another room. When he describes the divorce, he does not blame her. He says, quietly, “She got tired of living inside my perimeter.”

In the present, captivity still shapes ordinary moments. He avoids basements, storage rooms, windowless elevators, and any route that leaves him feeling trapped. Grocery shopping can become overwhelming if an aisle is crowded and he cannot see a clear path out. He scans every room automatically, noting exits, people’s hands, changes in voice. He keeps his phone charged, his cupboards overstocked, and his shoes lined up by the bed. On especially bad nights he sits awake at the kitchen table, listening to the building settle, unable to convince his body that silence means safety rather than danger.

He is troubled not only by fear but by the way his emotions narrowed after the ordeal. He used to enjoy travel, football with friends, the abstract challenge of market analysis. Now pleasure feels remote, as if his mind allows only vigilance or exhaustion. He speaks with guilt about others he met in captivity, wondering why he was released when he cannot be sure what happened to them. Sometimes a client’s cologne, a foreign-language news clip, or the click of a lock can drag him abruptly into the past. In those moments he is no longer a financial analyst reviewing quarterly variance reports; he is again a man in a small room, listening hard, waiting for footsteps, bracing for whatever comes next.
